title: Triggering CSS Animations on Scroll With No JavaScript
summary: Create CSS scroll-triggered animations without JavaScript. See syntax, trigger actions, scroll boundaries, and progressive enhancement with an IntersectionObserver fallback.
body_markdown:
Scroll-triggered animations let scrolling decide when a normal CSS animation begins. Once an element reaches a set scroll position, the animation plays on its own clock. You declare them with the` timeline-trigger` and` animation-trigger` properties, and no IntersectionObserver is needed.


Most “fade in on scroll” code looks the same everywhere: an observer, a threshold, a class toggle, and an` unobserve()` call that someone forgets to add. That work can now be done in CSS.


This article covers the syntax, one complete reveal example, the three trigger behaviours, how to pick scroll boundaries, and how to ship the feature safely in a Chromium-only world.


## Key Takeaways


- A scroll-triggered animation needs two declarations.` timeline-trigger` names a trigger and sets the scroll range that activates it.` animation-trigger` tells an animation which trigger to follow and what to do when it fires.
- The range` entry 100% exit 0%` activates a trigger only while the element is fully inside the scrollport. Chrome’s documentation treats it as equivalent to the` contain` keyword.
- ` play-forwards play-backwards` plays the animation on entry and reverses it on exit.` play-once` , from the Animation Triggers draft, runs it a single time.
- A triggered animation keeps its own duration and easing, so scrolling faster does not make it play faster.
- Chrome’s support data lists only Chromium browsers for scroll-triggered animations, so hide content inside` @supports` and keep an IntersectionObserver fallback.


## What Is the Difference Between Scroll-Driven and Scroll-Triggered Animations?


Scroll-driven animations tie an animation’s progress to scroll position. Scroll-triggered animations use scrolling only to decide when an ordinary animation starts. Our guide on how to[create scroll animations with just CSS](https://blog.openreplay.com/create-scroll-animations-with-just-css/) covers the first model:` animation-timeline` with` scroll()` and` view()` . There, the timeline replaces the clock, so scrolling back plays the animation in reverse. This article covers` timeline-trigger` and` animation-trigger` , which start a regular animation, with its own duration, once the element reaches a chosen scroll range.


If you want a reading-progress bar or parallax, use[CSS scroll progress animations](https://blog.openreplay.com/css-scroll-progress-animations/) . If you want a card to fade in over 400ms once it is visible, use a trigger. In its[Google I/O 2026 Web UI roundup](https://developer.chrome.com/blog/new-in-web-ui-io26) , Chrome lists the two as separate features and describes triggers as a way to replace IntersectionObserver with CSS. Put simply, a trigger is the CSS version of “add a class when this element becomes visible.”


## A Scroll-Triggered Fade-In Example


A scroll-triggered fade-in needs three parts: a` @keyframes` rule, an` animation` with` forwards` fill, and a trigger linking the animation to a view timeline. The[Chrome announcement of scroll-triggered animations](https://developer.chrome.com/blog/scroll-triggered-animations) defines the syntax. Its main points are that the trigger and the animation can sit on different elements, and that a trigger uses a scroll or view progress timeline as its source.


```text
<  section   class  =  "  reveal  "  >
<  div   class  =  "  reveal-content  "  >
<  h2  >  Shipping notes  </  h2  >
<  p  >  This block fades and slides in once it is fully on screen.  </  p  >
</  div  >
</  section  >
```


```text
@keyframes   reveal   {
to {
opacity  :   1  ;
translate  :   0   0  ;
}
}


@supports (timeline-trigger-name: --t) {
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {
.  reveal   {
timeline-trigger: --reveal view() entry 100% exit 0%;
trigger-scope: --reveal;
}


.  reveal-content   {
opacity  :   0  ;
translate  :   0   2rem  ;
animation  : reveal   400ms   ease-out   forwards  ;
animation-trigger: --reveal play-forwards;
}
}
}
```


How it works:


- **The trigger sits on the section and the motion on its child.** The element that slides is not the element whose visibility is measured, so the` translate` offset cannot move the trigger boundary.
- **` entry 100% exit 0%`** activates the trigger once the section is fully inside the scrollport.
- **` play-forwards`** starts the animation each time the trigger activates.` forwards` fill holds the final keyframe afterwards.
- **The hidden start state lives inside the feature query.** Browsers without support never apply` opacity: 0` , so content stays visible.
- **` trigger-scope`** keeps each section’s` --reveal` name local. By default any element on the page can see a trigger name, the same way` anchor-name` works, as the[Chrome 146 release notes](https://developer.chrome.com/release-notes/146) describe.


With` play-forwards` alone, leaving the range does nothing: the element keeps its end state as you scroll away. When it becomes fully visible again, the trigger activates again and the animation replays. The next section shows how to change that.


## Choosing a Trigger Action


` animation-trigger` accepts a trigger name followed by up to two actions. The first runs when the trigger activates and the second runs when it deactivates. The action you pick decides what happens on re-entry and on exit.


Desired behaviour` animation-trigger` value Note


Replay on every re-entry` --reveal play-forwards` Can visibly jump back to the start state


Reverse on exit` --reveal play-forwards play-backwards` After reversing, the element shows its base styles


Run once, then stay` --reveal play-once` Draft keyword, may change


```text
animation-trigger  : --reveal   play-forwards   play-backwards  ;   /* reverses on exit */
animation-trigger  : --reveal   play-once  ;   /* runs once; Animation Triggers draft keyword */
```


` forwards` fill holds the` to` keyframe after` play-forwards` finishes. It does not hold anything after` play-backwards` finishes. At that point the animation stops applying and the element falls back to its base styles. In this example the base styles are the hidden start state (` opacity: 0; translate: 0 2rem` ), because the keyframes define only` to` , so the element still ends up hidden. If your keyframes set a` from` state that differs from the base styles, use` both` so that state is held after the reverse.` play-once` comes from the[CSS Animation Triggers Level 1 Editor’s Draft](https://drafts.csswg.org/animation-triggers-1/) , not from Chrome’s announcement, so check it in your target Chrome build before relying on it. It is the closest match to calling` unobserve()` after the first intersection.


### Activation Range vs Active Range


In a scroll trigger, the activation range decides when the trigger fires. The optional active range, written after a slash, decides how long the trigger stays active, and Chrome requires it to enclose the activation range. According to Chrome,` entry 100% exit 0%` equals` contain` and` entry 0% exit 100%` equals` cover` , so these two lines are the same:


```text
timeline-trigger  : --reveal view() entry 100% exit 0% / entry 0% exit 100%;
timeline-trigger  : --reveal view() contain / cover;
```


With this setting, the trigger turns on once the element is fully in view and stays on until no part of it is visible. This matters for` play-backwards` , because the reverse animation waits until the element is off screen.


## Picking Sensible Scroll Boundaries


The right scroll-trigger range depends on the element’s size and on any fixed UI covering the viewport.


Situation Range Why


Small card or heading` entry 100% exit 0%` (` contain` ) Fires once the whole element is visible


Tall section` entry 25% exit 0%`` contain` may fire late for tall elements


Under a 4rem sticky header` view(block 4rem 0)` Stops the header from hiding the element


```text
/* Tall element: fire when a quarter has entered */
timeline-trigger  : --reveal view() entry 25% exit 0%;


/* 4rem sticky header: start (top) inset first */
timeline-trigger  : --reveal view(block 4rem 0) entry 100% exit 0%;
```


In[view()](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Reference/Properties/animation-timeline/view) , the start inset comes before the end inset. On a vertical block axis the start is the top, so a top header’s height goes first.


## Browser Support and Fallbacks


Chrome’s[Google I/O 2026 Web UI roundup](https://developer.chrome.com/blog/new-in-web-ui-io26) lists support for scroll-triggered animations in Chrome and Edge 146, with no support in Firefox or Safari. Chrome’s December 2025 announcement said the feature would land in Chrome 145, but it shipped in Chrome 146 (stable release 10 March 2026). The[Chrome 146 beta post](https://developer.chrome.com/blog/chrome-146-beta) lists` trigger-scope` in the same release. Treat the whole feature as progressive enhancement.


The` @supports` wrapper in the example handles this. Unsupported browsers skip the whole block and render the content statically. If you want the same motion in other browsers, keep your existing IntersectionObserver class toggle outside the feature query, and run it only when` CSS.supports()` returns false. Our piece on[replacing animation libraries with native web APIs](https://blog.openreplay.com/replace-animation-libraries-native-web-apis/) covers building that fallback without AOS-style dependencies.


The` prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference` query means users who ask for less motion see content immediately. To stagger several elements, point their` animation-trigger` at one shared trigger with different delays.


## Conclusion


Scroll-triggered animations cover the fade-in-on-scroll pattern: CSS decides when an ordinary animation starts, and the browser does the observing. Start with the example above. Choose the action (replay, reverse or run once) that matches your design, adjust the range for tall elements or sticky headers, and remove the observer code from supporting browsers while leaving it in place for the rest.


## FAQs


What is the difference between scroll-triggered animations and scroll-state container queries?


Scroll-state container queries apply styles while a container is in a browser-managed scroll state. Scroll-triggered animations start a keyframe animation when an element crosses a range on a view or scroll timeline. Chrome 133 shipped the stuck, snapped and scrollable states, and Chrome 144 added scrolled, which tracks the most recent scroll direction. Use a scroll-state query for a sticky header that restyles once stuck, and a trigger for reveal effects.


Are scroll-triggered animations faster than an IntersectionObserver reveal?


Chrome's release notes say that because the interaction is described in CSS, the browser can hand the work to a worker thread. An IntersectionObserver reveal runs its callback and class toggle on the main thread, so heavy script work can delay it. Chrome describes the offloading as a design benefit, not a measured result, so profile your own pages before and after the switch instead of assuming a gain.


Can scroll triggers control animations created with the Web Animations API?


Yes. The Chrome 146 release notes say the feature comes with JavaScript interfaces, so triggers can drive animations made with the Web Animations API and not only CSS animations. The interface names are defined in the CSS Animation Triggers Level 1 Editor's Draft, which can still change, so check the draft and your target Chrome build before relying on them.


Why does my element stay hidden after adding a scroll trigger?


The hidden start state applies as soon as the feature query matches, so the element stays at opacity 0 until its trigger activates. Common causes are a spelling mismatch between the timeline-trigger name and the animation-trigger name, an animated element outside the subtree set by trigger-scope, or a range the element never reaches. Check the name first, then confirm the animated element sits inside the scoping element.
